title: Abstract
text:
Abstract




High landscape connectivity supports the conservation of large mammals, but for wild boar (Sus scrofa) it also promotes the geographic spread of African Swine Fever (ASF), a viral disease with a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent and no available vaccine. As ASF expands westward across Europe, wildlife and veterinary authorities in Switzerland need spatially explicit tools that show how landscape interventions such as fences or wildlife crossings would change wild boar movement and disease spread risk. Existing connectivity models for the Swiss Mittelland are rigorous but static, and they cannot answer interactive scenario questions.
This thesis develops a species-specific resistance surface for wild boar and an interactive QGIS plugin that lets users test landscape modifications without programming knowledge. The resistance surface was calibrated empirically from GPS telemetry of 16 wild boar tracked in Canton Aargau between 2014 and 2017. Directed transit movements were separated from resting behaviour with a rule-based classifier, and an integrated step-selection function estimated habitat preferences from 7,810 transit steps. The selection coefficients were converted into a 25-metre resistance raster using the Keeley exponential transformation, and the calibrated model was transferred to Canton Zürich without re-estimation. The plugin combines five complementary analyses on the resulting surface: least-cost path corridors, circuit-theory pinch points, a cost-distance infection-risk kernel anchored to the EFSA operational zones, a biased correlated random walk, and an iSSF-based individual movement model of disease spread.
Seven landscape covariates were significant positive predictors of transit movement, with forest density at the local scale and distance to railway showing the strongest effects. The resulting resistance surfaces reproduce the known corridor structure of both cantons, concentrating low resistance along forested slopes and riparian zones. The plugin runs all five analyses in under three minutes and reacts correctly to user-placed fences and crossings, redistributing modelled corridors and contracting infection-risk zones in response. The tool is best understood as a pre-outbreak planning instrument that helps authorities identify priority fence locations before an ASF incursion occurs. Its main limitation is the absence of independent validation in the Zürich transfer area, which remains the most important next step.

Zusammenfassung
Eine hohe Landschaftskonnektivität unterstützt den Schutz grosser Säugetiere, fördert beim Wildschwein (Sus scrofa) jedoch zugleich die geografische Ausbreitung der Afrikanischen Schweinepest (ASP), einer Viruserkrankung mit einer Letalität von 90 bis 95 Prozent und ohne verfügbaren Impfstoff. Da sich die ASP in Europa weiter nach Westen ausbreitet, benötigen Wildhut und Veterinärbehörden in der Schweiz räumlich explizite Werkzeuge, die zeigen, wie sich bauliche Eingriffe wie Zäune oder Wildtierüberführungen auf die Bewegung von Wildschweinen und das Ausbreitungsrisiko auswirken. Die bestehenden Konnektivitätsmodelle für das Schweizer Mittelland sind methodisch fundiert, aber statisch und erlauben keine interaktive Szenarienanalyse.
Diese Arbeit entwickelt eine artspezifische Widerstandsoberfläche für das Wildschwein sowie ein interaktives QGIS-Plugin, mit dem Anwenderinnen und Anwender ohne Programmierkenntnisse Landschaftsveränderungen testen können. Die Widerstandsoberfläche wurde empirisch aus GPS-Telemetriedaten von 16 Wildschweinen kalibriert, die zwischen 2014 und 2017 im Kanton Aargau besendert wurden. Gerichtete Wanderbewegungen wurden mit einem regelbasierten Klassifikator vom Ruheverhalten getrennt, und eine integrierte Step-Selection-Funktion schätzte die Habitatpräferenzen aus 7810 Transitschritten. Die Selektionskoeffizienten wurden mit der exponentiellen Keeley-Transformation in ein 25-Meter-Widerstandsraster überführt, und das kalibrierte Modell wurde ohne Neuschätzung auf den Kanton Zürich übertragen. Das Plugin verbindet fünf sich ergänzende Analysen: Least-Cost-Path-Korridore, Engstellen aus der Schaltkreistheorie, einen distanzbasierten Infektionsrisiko-Kernel entlang der EFSA-Zonen, einen biased correlated random walk sowie ein iSSF-basiertes individuenbasiertes Ausbreitungsmodell.
Sieben Landschaftsvariablen waren signifikante positive Prädiktoren der Transitbewegung, wobei die lokale Walddichte und die Distanz zur Bahnlinie die stärksten Effekte zeigten. Die resultierenden Widerstandsoberflächen geben die bekannte Korridorstruktur beider Kantone wieder und konzentrieren geringe Widerstände entlang bewaldeter Hänge und Gewässerräume. Das Plugin führt alle fünf Analysen in weniger als drei Minuten aus und reagiert korrekt auf von Nutzenden platzierte Zäune und Überführungen, indem es die modellierten Korridore umverteilt und die Risikozonen verkleinert. Das Werkzeug eignet sich vor allem als Planungsinstrument vor einem Ausbruch und hilft den Behörden, prioritäre Zaunstandorte frühzeitig zu bestimmen. Die wichtigste Einschränkung ist die fehlende unabhängige Validierung im Übertragungsgebiet Zürich, die den zentralen nächsten Schritt darstellt.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Problem Statement
The Swiss Mittelland is among the most densely settled and intensively managed landscapes in Central Europe. Roads, railways, urban expansion and intensive agriculture collectively form a network of barriers that fragments natural habitats and restricts the free movement of wildlife across the region. For large mammals, this fragmentation carries serious long-term consequences: reduced population exchange, diminishing genetic diversity and a decline in regional population viability (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023). In a landscape as structurally altered as the Canton of Zurich, restoring meaningful ecological connectivity is therefore an active and ongoing challenge for wildlife managers and spatial planners.
In response, spatial planning frequently relies on targeted structural interventions such as wildlife overpasses and underpasses, whose effectiveness for species like red deer (Cervus elaphus) has been documented across Switzerland and neighbouring France (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023). Assessing where such infrastructure is most needed requires spatially explicit connectivity models. Robust frameworks for this purpose have been established and validated at the regional scale by Urbina et al. (2023) and, more recently, for the Swiss Mittelland by Fischer et al. (2024), producing maps of movement corridors, pinch points and connectivity bottlenecks that can directly guide conservation planning.
What these models have not yet addressed is a parallel management challenge. Unlike red deer, the wild boar (Sus scrofa) is not primarily a species in need of connectivity enhancement. It is the primary wildlife reservoir of African Swine Fever (ASF), a viral disease with a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent in infected animals for which no effective vaccine exists (Guberti et al. 2019). High landscape connectivity for wild boar directly facilitates the geographic spread of ASF, meaning that interventions designed to benefit species like red deer can simultaneously increase disease transmission risk for wild boar across the same landscape.
This conflict between promoting connectivity for conservation and restricting it to prevent disease spread is not new to ecological theory. Hess (1994) demonstrated formally that conservation corridors can, under certain epidemiological conditions, dramatically increase the risk of disease-driven population extinction. The epidemiology of ASF in wild boar matches those conditions closely enough to make this trade-off a concrete management problem for wildlife authorities, particularly as ASF continues to expand its range westward across Europe.
The connectivity models developed by Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023) are methodologically rigorous and well validated, but they are static representations of the current landscape. They do not allow practitioners to test hypothetical scenarios interactively. A wildlife manager or veterinary authority asking what would happen to ASF spread risk if a fence were installed along a specific road, or what connectivity a proposed wildlife overpass would deliver for red deer, currently has no tool to answer that question dynamically. This gap between analytical capability and operational decision support is the direct motivation for this thesis.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Objectives
This thesis develops an interactive spatial planning tool in the form of a QGIS plugin that models functional connectivity for wild boar across the Canton of Zurich. The plugin allows users to dynamically alter the underlying landscape resistance surface by placing hypothetical infrastructure elements, such as movement barriers or wildlife crossings, directly on the map. After each modification, the model recalculates the resulting connectivity and visualises the effect on potential ASF spread corridors and pinch points. The underlying methodology adapts the resistance surface construction, least-cost path calculation and circuit-theory-based corridor modeling approach of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023), with all parameters specifically tailored to the ecology and movement behaviour of wild boar.
Two specific objectives guide this work. The first is the methodological adaptation of the existing connectivity modeling framework for wild boar, including the classification of wild boar telemetry data into in-matrix and in-patch movement, the fitting of an integrated Step Selection Function based on spatial covariantes and finally the construction of a species-specific resistance surface. The second is the development of an interactive QGIS plugin that allows end users to simulate ASF spread from a specific location with different connectivity models and structural landscape changes without requiring programming knowledge.

title: 2  Theoretical Background
text:
2.1 Ecological Connectivity in Fragmented Landscapes
This chapter sets out the concepts the thesis relies on: landscape connectivity and its modeling, the movement ecology of wild boar, and the epidemiology of African Swine Fever (ASF), which together make connectivity a key factor in disease management.
Landscape connectivity describes the degree to which a landscape facilitates or impedes the movement of organisms among habitat patches. Taylor et al. (1993) formalised the concept as a vital structural element of landscapes, and it is now standard to separate two dimensions. Structural connectivity refers to the physical arrangement of habitat in space and can be read from land cover maps alone. Functional connectivity reflects the behavioural response of a specific species to that structure (Urbina et al. 2023; Tischendorf et al. 2003), so two structurally identical landscapes can differ greatly depending on whether the target species treats roads, rivers, or fields as permeable or as barriers. A resistance surface calibrated for one species therefore cannot simply be reused for another. This distinction matters in the Swiss Mittelland, which looks connected on a coarse map but is functionally fragmented for large mammals by dense road and rail networks, urban development, and intensive agriculture, leading to reduced gene flow and limited recolonisation for species such as red deer and wild boar (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023).

title: 2  Theoretical Background
text:
2.2 Modeling Functional Connectivity
The following section provides a theoretical explanation of all the modeling methods for functional connectivity used in this study.

2.2.1 Resistance Surfaces and the Integrated Step-Selection Function
The resistance surface is the core spatial input to all functional connectivity models. It is a raster in which each cell carries a value representing the relative cost of movement, with high-quality habitat assigned low resistance and barriers such as motorways assigned very high or infinite resistance. Resistance can be assigned from expert judgement or, more defensibly, estimated empirically from GPS tracking. Urbina et al. (2023) derived resistance for red deer from over 85,000 GPS fixes of 15 individuals across the Greater Geneva agglomeration at 5-metre resolution, and Fischer et al. (2024) applied a comparable empirical framework to the Swiss Mittelland. Finer resolution resolves the narrow infrastructure that constrains large-mammal movement but multiplies the cell count and the computational cost.
Where GPS data are available, the integrated step-selection function (iSSF) provides a principled basis for the empirical approach (Avgar et al. 2016). The iSSF reconstructs movement as a sequence of steps, each with a step length and turning angle, and compares every observed step against random alternatives drawn from the same movement kernel. Fitting a conditional logistic regression of the form \(w(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\!\left(\sum_k \hat{\beta}_k x_k\right)\), where \(w(\mathbf{x})\) is the relative selection strength of a step ending at covariate values \(x_k\) and \(\hat{\beta}_k\) is the estimated selection coefficient for covariate \(k\), yields coefficients that express habitat preference while holding movement capacity and availability constant. This separates genuine preference from mere abundance: an animal seen often in forest may prefer forest, or forest may simply be plentiful where it started, and the conditional design distinguishes the two. The fitted linear predictor is rescaled into a habitat suitability \(S \in [0, 1]\), which Keeley et al. (2016) proposed to convert into resistance through the negative exponential transformation \(R = \exp\!\left(c \cdot (1 - S)\right)\), where \(c\) is a positive constant that controls how sharply resistance increases as suitability declines. A single tracking dataset therefore yields a resistance surface that is both species-specific and statistically grounded.

Left: at each observed location the animal’s realised step (solid arrow) is compared against random available steps (dashed arrows) drawn from its movement kernel, so the model learns which features are selected. Right: the fitted coefficients are translated into a resistance raster, where preferred habitat receives low resistance (green) and barriers such as roads receive high resistance (red).







2.2.2 Least-Cost Paths and Circuit Theory
Least-cost path (LCP) analysis was among the first methods to use resistance surfaces for corridor mapping (Adriaensen et al. 2003). It identifies the single route between two patches that minimises cumulative resistance. It is computationally cheap and widely used, but it assumes movement along one optimal route and says nothing about whether alternative routes exist or how redundant the surrounding landscape is (McRae et al. 2008).
Circuit theory addresses that limitation by treating the resistance surface as an electrical network in which current flows from a source to a ground through all available pathways at once (McRae et al. 2008). McRae et al. (2008) showed that the current through any cell is proportional to the expected number of times a random walker would pass through it, giving the method a process-based interpretation that LCP lacks. High current density marks heavily used corridors, and points where the landscape forces nearly all movement through a single passage are called pinch points, which are the highest-priority targets for intervention because losing a small area there disproportionately reduces connectivity. Because effective resistance falls as parallel routes are added, the method also captures redundancy, and the ratio of least-cost to resistance distance measures how much a single bottleneck dominates. The Circuitscape software solves networks of millions of cells, making it applicable at landscape scale. Urbina et al. (2023) applied Circuitscape 5 to a graph of 172 core areas and 424 links in Greater Geneva, mapping the major corridors and confirming the role of specific wildlife overpasses.








Figure 2.2: Schematic comparison of least-cost path (LCP) and circuit-theory corridor modelling applied to the same resistance surface. Left: The LCP analysis identifies a single optimal route (red line) connecting the source (S) and destination (D) patches by minimising cumulative movement cost, threading through the narrow low-resistance gap between the two high-resistance blocks (dark grey). Right: Circuit theory treats the same surface as a resistor network and lets current flow from source to destination through all possible pathways simultaneously. The resulting current density (Magma ramp) does not single out one route but reveals the relative importance of the entire corridor network, concentrating at the pinch point where the landscape forces movement through the narrow passage.







2.2.3 Infection-Risk Kernels and Cost-Distance Dispersal
An infection-risk kernel converts a cost-distance analysis into the probability that a dispersing infected animal reaches a given location before dying. Dispersal is described by an exponential kernel \(P(d) = \exp(-d/D)\), where \(d\) is a distance measure and \(D\) is a characteristic dispersal scale set from telemetry. The single parameter \(D\) has a direct probabilistic interpretation and can be read from the literature. For wild boar, the relevant scale during the infectious period is the mean natal dispersal distance rather than the home-range diameter, because infected animals move normally until the final clinical phase. Telemetry and mark-recapture studies across European populations report mean dispersal of approximately 4 kilometres, with most events within 10 kilometres of the birth site (Truvé and Lemel 2003; Keuling et al. 2010; Prévot and Licoppe 2013; Morelle et al. 2015). Critically, \(d\) is taken as Dijkstra cost-distance through the resistance surface rather than straight-line distance, so the kernel assigns near-zero risk to cells that are geographically close but separated by a motorway or large water body. The EFSA operational framework gives a validation benchmark (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018): the 3-kilometre protection zone corresponds to a risk of about 0.50 under the kernel with \(D = 4\) km, and the 10-kilometre surveillance boundary to about 0.08, which lets the displayed risk classes be anchored to recognised thresholds.








Figure 2.3: Schematic of the cost-distance infection-risk kernel. Risk decays exponentially from the outbreak origin. Because distance is measured through the resistance surface rather than in a straight line, a barrier casts a low-risk shadow: location B, behind the barrier, carries far lower risk than location A at the same straight-line distance in open terrain. Dashed and dotted circles mark the EFSA protection (about 3 km) and surveillance (about 10 km) thresholds.







2.2.4 Biased Correlated Random Walk
A biased correlated random walk (BCRW) models movement as discrete steps shaped by two forces: directional memory, which correlates successive steps, and an environmental bias toward low-cost terrain (Turchin 1998; Codling et al. 2008). Directional persistence is described by the von Mises distribution, where the probability of a turn \(\theta\) is proportional to \(\exp(\kappa \cos\theta)\) and the concentration \(\kappa\) controls how strongly the walker continues in its current direction. Weighting each candidate step by the inverse of destination resistance and step length adds the cost bias. As the number of walks grows, the BCRW visit density converges toward the circuit-theory current map under the Randomized Shortest Paths equivalence (panzacchi2016?), so the two methods estimate the same quantity by different means. In practice this limit is reached only with very many walks, which makes the BCRW a useful complementary diagnostic rather than a replacement for circuit theory.








Figure 2.4: Schematic of a biased correlated random walk. Several stochastic trajectories start from the same source. Directional persistence keeps successive steps roughly aligned, while a bias toward low-cost terrain steers the walks along the low-resistance corridor (green band). Accumulated over many walks, the visit density approximates the circuit-theory current map.







2.2.5 Individual-Based Movement Models
Individual-based movement models take a finer-grained approach by reconstructing movement one step at a time and asking which landscape conditions at the end of each step the animal preferentially selects (Avgar et al. 2016). The integrated step-selection function (iSSF) introduced above is the most widely used method in this class, and the same machinery that calibrates the resistance surface can also drive a forward simulation of individual trajectories. Rather than solving for a global flow as circuit theory does, an iSSF-based individual-based movement model (IBMM) releases simulated agents into the landscape and lets each one move according to the fitted step-length and turning-angle kernels, selecting successive cells in proportion to their estimated habitat suitability. Because the suitability surface is recovered directly from the iSSF coefficients, the simulated paths reflect the same empirically estimated preferences that define the resistance surface, which makes the IBMM a behaviourally explicit complement to the aggregate corridor methods. Its particular value for disease work is that each agent can be given a finite lifespan drawn from an infectious-period distribution, so the accumulated visit pattern estimates how far an infected animal is likely to spread contamination before dying rather than only where movement is possible (Avgar et al. 2016).








Figure 2.5: Schematic of the iSSF-based individual-based movement model. Left: simulated agents move step by step according to the fitted movement and habitat-selection kernels, with each trajectory ending when the agent’s drawn infectious-period lifespan elapses (square endpoints). The inset fan at one location illustrates how, at every step, the model draws 25 candidate ‘available’ steps from the fitted step-length and turning-angle kernels (dotted grey) and selects the realised ‘used’ step (solid black) in proportion to its estimated habitat suitability. Right: accumulating these finite-lifespan trajectories over many agents yields a spatial footprint of how far and in which directions contamination is likely to spread from the source before the agents die.

section: 2.3 Wild Boar Ecology Relevant to Connectivity
text:
2.3 Wild Boar Ecology Relevant to Connectivity
The wild boar (Sus scrofa) is a native Eurasian ungulate whose European populations have expanded strongly in recent decades, driven by milder winters, the spread of maize and other high-energy crops, reduced hunting pressure, and supplementary winter feeding (Guberti et al. 2019). Wild boar are habitat generalists that use woodland, especially deciduous and mixed forest, as daytime resting cover and forage at night in agricultural fields, showing marked behavioural flexibility in fragmented and peri-urban landscapes (Morelle et al. 2015). This forest dependence for cover and avoidance of human infrastructure is what a resistance surface must capture. Home ranges are usually well below 50 square kilometres and movement contracts where food is stable and abundant (Guberti et al. 2019; Morelle et al. 2015). The epidemiologically important exception is natal dispersal by young males, which can cover much greater distances and, rarely, exceed 100 kilometres (Guberti et al. 2019), because a dispersing animal in the incubation phase can carry infection into previously unaffected areas.

section: 2.4 African Swine Fever and the Connectivity Trade-off
text:
2.4 African Swine Fever and the Connectivity Trade-off
ASF is caused by a large DNA virus of the family Asfarviridae that in Europe affects only domestic pigs and wild boar (Guberti et al. 2019). The genotype II strain of the current epidemic has a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent, most infected animals die within four to nine days of showing signs, and no licensed vaccine exists, so control depends on surveillance, movement restriction, and population management. The virus is exceptionally stable, remaining infectious in blood for up to 15 weeks and persisting in carcasses for months, so infected carcasses act as long-lived reservoirs that decouple persistence from host density (Guberti et al. 2019). Transmission runs through direct contact, which depends on host density, and through contact with carcasses and fomites, which sustains the cycle even as the live population declines. Since its introduction to the Caucasus in 2007, ASF has advanced westward at roughly 1 to 3 kilometres per month through wild boar populations, with human-induced outbreaks that form new clusters ahead of the front, leaving currently disease-free countries including Switzerland at near-term risk (Guberti et al. 2019).
The more connected and continuous the wild boar population, the faster the epidemic spread advances, while natural or artificial barriers can slow it. This makes connectivity a genuine management variable: authorities can in principle reduce spread by reinforcing barriers, installing targeted fencing in high-connectivity areas, or lowering density in specific corridors. Doing so effectively requires knowing where the corridors and pinch points are and predicting how an intervention would change them. Hess (1994) provided formal support for this and demonstrated that conservation corridors generally aid metapopulation persistence but, under conditions of high direct-contact transmission and high disease-induced mortality that closely match ASF, can substantially raise the risk of disease-driven extinction. The same corridors that benefit red deer can therefore accelerate ASF in wild boar. Existing models, including those of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023), are rigorous but static and cannot answer what-if questions about a proposed fence or overpass. Building a tool that combines their methodological rigour with interactive, user-defined scenarios for wild boar in the Canton of Zürich is the central task of this thesis.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.1 Software Environment and Data Inputs
The methodology has two phases. The first builds an empirically calibrated wild boar resistance surface from GPS telemetry. The second translates that surface into an interactive QGIS plugin. Full dataset information is given in ?sec-data, and the complete parameter settings of the plugin modules are listed in the statistical appendix.
The ecological algorithm was developed in R 4.5.1, using terra and sf for spatial handling, amt for movement metrics and step generation, the tidyverse packages for data wrangling, survival for the conditional logistic regression, and car for collinearity diagnostics. The plugin was implemented in Python for QGIS 3.40.13 as Wildboar Connectivity (ASF), version 0.6. It builds on the QGIS API (qgis.core, qgis.gui, qgis.PyQt) for the interface, map tools and layer handling, numpy and rasterio for raster reading, writing and georeferencing, and scipy for the sparse-matrix circuit-theory solver and connected-component analysis that underlie the pinchpoint and least-cost-path modules. Circuit-theory pinchpoint analysis is primarily delegated to the official Julia package Circuitscape.jl, invoked as an external subprocess, with the scipy-based solver serving as a fallback when Julia is not available on the user’s system. Exact package versions are listed in the reproducibility appendix.
Canton Aargau served as the training area where the resistance model was calibrated, and Canton Zürich as the independent transfer area where the plugin was evaluated. A master raster grid was generated for each canton in the Swiss LV95 reference system (EPSG:2056) at 25-metre resolution. To avoid edge effects, each cantonal boundary was buffered by 1,000 metres and converted to a rectangular processing extent, which was then intersected with the national boundary because the high-resolution covariates are restricted to Swiss territory. Extending the study area into Germany was rejected because harmonising Swiss and German topographic and land cover data would have required reconciling incompatible classifications and resolutions, and pan-European products such as CORINE are too coarse to resolve the narrow forest corridors and minor roads that govern wild boar movement at a 15-minute fix interval.
The biological foundation was a GPS telemetry dataset of 16 wild boar tracked in the Aargau study area between 2014 and 2017 at a 15-minute interval, collected by the Wildlife Management Research Group (WILMA, ZHAW) in the Wildschweinschreck project. This dataset enabled a strictly empirical resistance surface rather than one based on expert opinion. Environmental covariates were derived from swissTLM3D (2026 edition) for forest, roads, railways, settlements, and water, and from the DHM25 elevation model for terrain. Administrative extents came from swissBOUNDARIES3D. Three further datasets supported the transfer to Zürich. The national wildlife passages geodatabase from the FOEN was used to restore permeability at verified crossings. The permanent ASP fence shapefile from the WILMA research group was used as an absolute barrier. The WILMA potential core-habitat layer for Zürich was used as least-cost-path targets. The role, version, and coordinate system of each dataset are tabulated in the data sources appendix ?sec-data.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.2 Resistance Surface Pipeline
The pipeline runs in three stages: preprocessing and behavioural classification of the telemetry data, empirical estimation of habitat preference with an iSSF, and transformation of the coefficients into resistance with the Keeley et al. (2016) exponential function. The design follows the connectivity frameworks of Fischer et al. (2024), Clontz et al. (2021), and Keeley et al. (2016).

3.2.1 Telemetry Processing and Step Classification
All geometries were standardised to LV95. Records with missing or implausible coordinates were removed, timestamps were standardised to UTC, and the first five days of each deployment were dropped as a capture-shock buffer. Deployments with fewer than 100 fixes or spanning under 30 days were excluded, as were the fixes with a biologically unrealistic step length (> 3000m) (Podgórski et al. 2013). Trajectories were resampled to a 15-minute interval with a five-minute tolerance and segmented into temporally continuous bursts, so that step lengths and turning angles were never computed across a data gap.
Because a resistance surface models the cost of travelling between habitat patches rather than behaviour within them, the steps were separated into in-patch (stationary, resting, foraging) and in-matrix (movement, directed transit, migration) states. The fractal and mixture-model approach used for red deer by Fischer et al. (2024) proved unsuitable, because wild boar are highly resident and their transit and resting modes are far less spatially separated than in migratory red deer. A rule-based classifier was therefore developed, applied within each burst, which labels a step as in-matrix if it meets any of three criteria. The first is a step length above 250 metres (Podgórski et al. 2013). The second is a step length above 150 metres combined with a turning angle below \(\pi/4\) in absolute value (Clontz et al. 2021). The third is three or more consecutive steps each above 100 metres with a turning angle below \(\pi/4\) (Benhamou 2014). All other steps were classified as in-patch, and only the in-matrix steps were retained for fitting.


3.2.2 Spatial Covariates
Covariates were derived on the 25-metre master grid using the buffered extent so that focal statistics near the boundary were unbiased.
A binary forest mask was created by extracting relevant forest classes (“Wald”, “Wald offen”, “Gebueschwald”, and “Gehoelzflaeche”) from the swissTLM3D layer ‘tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung’. During the rasterisation, the all-touched parameter ensured to preserve narrow tree lines. Then a 50-metre and a 1000-metre focal window was used to capture forest density. These two layers reflected immediate cover and broader landscape context, representing two different spatial orders of habitat selection (Johnson 1980). Furthermore a distance-to-forest-edge layer was defined to analyse the behaviour of wild boar in forests. This layer was created by calculating the euclidean distance from a pixel outside of the forest to the nearest forest pixel and inside the forest to the nearest non-forest pixel.
Topographic variables (slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index) were derived from the DHM25 digital elevation model using the terrain function. Because the raw ASCII file lacked an embedded Coordinate Reference System (CRS), the LV03 projection was explicitly assigned before cropping the data to the study area. After computing the terrain metrics, the resulting continuous layers were reprojected onto the LV95 master grid using bilinear interpolation.
Spatial data for standing and flowing water bodies were extracted from two highly detailed swissTLM3D layers (tlm_gewaesser_stehendes_gewaesser and tlm_gewaesser_fliessgewaesser). Because standing water features are natively structured as shoreline line strings, a custom geometric operation was applied to merge these segments and cast them into solid polygons. Known island geometries were explicitly subtracted from these features to accurately represent pure water surfaces. Flowing water features were filtered to retain only above-ground segments (e.g., surface flow, bridges, waterfalls), excluding subterranean conduits. Following rasterization, Euclidean distance layers were computed across the study extent for three distinct categories: all water bodies combined, standing water exclusively, and flowing water exclusively. Furthermore, a distinct binary mask was generated for large standing water bodies exceeding a 1km² threshold, allowing them to be included as absolute barriers in the resistance surface.
Spatial data representing human infrastructure were extracted from different swissTLM3D layers (tlm_strassen_strasse, tlm_oev_eisenbahn and tlm_namen_siedlungsname). To ensure only features acting as physical barriers or behavioral deterrents to wild boar were retained, the data underwent rigorous preprocessing. All three-dimensional geometries were flattened to 2D, and subterranean features (e.g., road and railway tunnels) were explicitly removed based on their elevation level and infrastructure type codes. Furthermore, railway networks were filtered to exclude disused tracks, funiculars, cog railways, and museum lines, as these do not constitute meaningful movement barriers. Road networks were hierarchically classified into fenced roads (highways), main roads, and secondary roads (e.g., local and forest tracks). Settlements were extracted as contiguous built-up polygons rather than individual building footprints. To model the effect of human proximity on habitat selection, continuous Euclidean distance rasters were generated for fenced roads, main roads, secondary roads, railways, and settlements. For subsequent connectivity modeling, infrastructure layers were categorized by their assumed permeability. Secondary roads were maintained solely as graded proximity covariates, as wild boar routinely cross narrow forest tracks. Conversely, a combined soft-barrier mask was generated comprising main roads, railways, and settlements. Fenced highways were isolated into a discrete binary mask to be parameterized as absolute movement barriers. Finally, known wildlife passages were imported, buffered by 30 meters to represent functional crossing zones, and rasterized to serve as localized permeability features capable of overriding absolute highway barriers.


3.2.3 Integrated Step-Selection Function
The Integrated Step Selection Function was fitted exclusively on the in matrix steps. Each observed step was compared against ten random control steps drawn from the empirical gamma step length and von Mises turning angle distributions, consistent with established practice (Avgar et al. 2016). Prior to model formulation, steps lacking angular measurements or exhibiting a length of exactly zero were excluded. Two movement kernel terms were included to ensure habitat selection was estimated independently of the underlying movement process: the cosine of the turning angle and the natural logarithm of the step length plus one. Covariate values were extracted at each step endpoint. All continuous covariates were standardized using the training mean and standard deviation from the Aargau data. These scaling parameters were saved to ensure the identical transformation could be applied to the Zurich projection.
A variable selection step removed seven of the fourteen candidate covariates. The seven retained ones, all demonstrated variance inflation factors below 1.4 and were therefore included in the final model. This final model was fitted using conditional logistic regression stratified by step ID, applying the Efron approximation for tied event times.


3.2.4 Resistance Surface Construction and Transfer
The conversion from selection coefficients to spatial resistance followed the three-stage framework outlined by Keeley et al. (2016). First, the linear predictor was calculated for every cell as the weighted sum of the scaled covariates:
\[\eta = \sum_k \hat{\beta}_k \cdot x_{k,\text{scaled}},\]
This predictor was normalized to a habitat suitability surface \(S \in [0,1]\) using local min-max scaling. Finally, suitability was transformed into a resistance surface using the negative exponential function:
\[R = \exp\!\left(C \cdot (1 - S)\right), \qquad C = 4,\]
A scaling constant of \(C = 4\) was applied (Fischer et al. 2024), yielding a theoretical resistance range from 1 for the optimal habitat to approximately 54.6 for the least preferred.
Following the continuous transformation, a deterministic burn-in assigned absolute values to discrete landscape features in a strict hierarchical order. Infrastructure cells comprising main roads, active railways, and settlements received the maximum continuous resistance value (\(R_{max}\)). Fenced motorways and large lakes (exceeding \(\text{1km}^2\)) were assigned as NoData to act as absolute, impassable barriers. Finally, verified wildlife passages were assigned the minimum resistance (\(R = 1\)), ensuring these specific mitigation structures remained fully permeable and actively overrode underlying highway barriers.
To project this model, the identical covariates were computed for the Canton Zürich extent. The linear predictor was calculated using the Aargau selection coefficients and scaling parameters without re-estimation. Crucially, the final normalization utilized the Zürich-specific linear predictor range rather than the Aargau baseline. This localized scaling ensures the full \([0,1]\) suitability spectrum is utilized, maximizing spatial contrast for within-Zürich corridor identification. While this approach renders absolute resistance values non-comparable across cantons, it is optimal for intra-cantonal connectivity planning. The burn-in hierarchy was applied identically to the Zürich surface, with the addition of permanent African Swine Fever (ASF) prevention fences, which were parameterized as absolute NoData barriers immediately prior to the wildlife passage burn-in.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.3 QGIS Plugin Development
The second phase translated the validated resistance surface into an interactive decision-support tool. The Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin lets a wildlife or veterinary user load the pre-computed resistance raster, define a hypothetical outbreak location with a map click, draw virtual fences or place wildlife overpasses on the canvas, and immediately recompute connectivity to compare scenarios. All computation runs in a background thread so the interface stays responsive.

3.3.1 Architecture and Interaction Model
The plugin is organised as cooperating Python modules with bounded responsibilities: an entry-point module that registers the plugin and owns the dialog and map tools, two custom map tools for point selection and polyline drawing, a stateless resistance-editor that returns a modified copy of the array without ever writing to the source raster, a background task that implements the five analyses, and a subprocess wrapper for the Circuitscape.jl solver. Communication between user actions and logic uses the Qt signal-and-slot mechanism, so the drawing tools carry out no computation themselves. The dialog exposes a resistance-raster selector, an optional habitat-polygon selector for least-cost-path targets, the three drawing tools, and five checkboxes selecting which analyses to run.


3.3.2 Landscape Modification
When the user runs an analysis, accumulated fences and overpasses are transformed into the raster coordinate system and applied to a deep copy of the loaded resistance window, so the source file is never altered. Fence polylines are rasterised with all-touched coverage and dilated to a two-cell-wide ribbon of NaN, making them indistinguishable from the absolute barriers already encoded in the surface. Overpasses are stamped as small discs of minimum resistance, and this overwrite is bidirectional, so an overpass placed on a motorway replaces the NaN with a passable value, correctly representing a crossing punched through an otherwise impassable structure.


3.3.3 Analysis Window, Source, and Cost Grid
The analysis is restricted to a window centred on the outbreak origin, extending 10,000 metres plus a 1,500-metre edge buffer in each direction and snapped to the integer pixel grid of the source so that outputs are not shifted relative to the input. The outbreak source is a disc of finite-resistance cells around the origin, snapped to the nearest passable cell if the click lands on a barrier. From the source disc, a single Dijkstra sweep computes the cost grid. The sweep uses an 8-connected metric that also penalises diagonal moves, so each reachable cell receives the lowest total cost of getting there from the origin. Cells behind absolute barriers stay at infinite cost. These unreachable cells mark the edge of the area of interest, the part of the landscape the outbreak can actually reach.


3.3.4 The Five Analyses
The least-cost path module connects the origin to the nearest reachable habitat clusters and traces each route back through the Dijkstra grid. These clusters are either taken from a user-supplied habitat layer or auto-detected by thresholding the resistance raster. Shared segments accumulate strength so that the backbone corridor serving many or large clusters is highlighted over the smaller corridors.
The infection-risk module converts the cost grid into a continuous probability surface, \(\text{risk}(d) = \exp(-d/D_{\text{cost}})\), where \(D_{\text{cost}}\) rescales the published 4-kilometre mean wild boar dispersal distance into cost units. This is done by using the pixel size and the median resistance of the window. The results are divided into three zones based on EFSA guidelines, with the high-risk category corresponding to the 3-kilometer protection zone and the medium-risk category corresponding to the 10-kilometer surveillance zone (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018).
The pinchpoint module treats the window as a resistor network and injects current from the source to the boundary, identifying where movement concentrates. The preferred solver is Circuitscape.jl, which is called as a Julia subprocess. A scipy Laplacian solver written entirely in Python is used as a fallback. Although it is slower, it produces equivalent results.
The biased correlated random walk releases many walkers from the source disc, each selecting steps by the product of a cost weight and a von Mises directional-persistence weight. Then it accumulates a visit-density surface that provides an independent stochastic check on the pinchpoint result (panzacchi2016?).
The iSSF-based individual movement model simulates infected animals from the origin. Each is running for a stochastically drawn infectious period and selecting steps by habitat suitability. In this case the habitat suitability is recovered by inverting the Keeley transformation, \(S = 1 - \ln R / C\) on the resistance surface. The fraction of animals visiting each cell gives a contamination-probability surface that quantifies disease reach rather than movement capacity alone. The infectious-period distribution and the movement-kernel parameters of these modules are calibrated to EFSA virological data and to ASF studies in European wild boar (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018; Probst et al. 2017; Chenais et al. 2019).

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1 Resistance Surface
Two primary deliverables were created during this project: a 25-metre resolution wild boar resistance surface covering Canton Aargau (used for model calibration) and Canton Zürich (produced by parameter transfer), and the Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) QGIS plugin that uses this resistance surface as its analytical input. The following sections present the results of this two steps.
In the following section the results of creating the resistance surface are shown and explained in detail.

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1.1 Telemetry Quality and Step Classification
Raw GPS telemetry data from 16 wild boar tracked in Canton Aargau between 2014 and 2017 were processed prior to trajectory analysis. Individuals with a tracking duration of less than 30 days or fewer than 100 total fixes were excluded from the dataset (n = 2). For the remaining 14 individuals (yielding 161,275 raw fixes), the trajectories were resampled to standardise the sampling frequency. A nominal 15-minute fix interval with a 5-minute tolerance was applied. Fixes that fell outside this 10 to 20-minute window, or redundant fixes within the same window, were dropped. This regularisation resulted in a 14.3% data loss (23,015 excluded fixes). Additionally, three biologically unrealistic step lengths (>3000m) were also dropped. The remaining 138,260 standardised fixes were subsequently converted into steps, yielding a final dataset of 133,109 continuous steps for analysis.
The three-rule hierarchical classifier partitioned these steps into 7,824 (5.9%) in-matrix transit steps and 125,285 (94.1%) in-patch resting steps. Among in-matrix steps, Rule 1 (step length greater than 250 metres) captured 4,759 steps (60.8% of all in-matrix steps), Rule 2 (step length greater than 150 metres and absolute turning angle below π/4 radians) contributed 2,748 steps (35.1%), and Rule 3 (three or more consecutive directional steps each exceeding 100 metres) added 317 steps (4.1%). The in-matrix dataset served as the sole analytical sample for iSSF fitting. In-patch steps were excluded from the model because they describe resting and foraging behaviour within habitat patches rather than landscape-level transit between patches, and combining the two behavioural states would confound the resistance surface.
In-matrix step lengths ranged from 100 metres to 2,840 metres with a mean of 298 metres, a median of 273 metres, and a standard deviation of 137 metres. The distribution is right-skewed, consistent with the gamma-distributed step-length kernel assumed by the iSSF movement model. Turning angles were approximately symmetric around zero with a standard deviation of approximately 59 degrees, indicating moderate directional persistence during transit. These values support the movement-kernel assumptions underlying the iSSF and confirm that the retained steps reflect directed transit rather than stationary behaviour.

title: 4  Results
text:
4.3 QGIS Plugin
The Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin was implemented as a QGIS 3.40 extension and tested against the Zürich resistance raster with the WILMA core habitat polygons as LCP destination targets. Functional testing confirmed that all five analytical modules produced spatially coherent outputs for a range of outbreak origin locations across the canton. Two scenarios are reported here: a baseline analysis at an unmodified outbreak location in a forested area, and a scenario comparison demonstrating the effect of drawing a virtual fence across a corridor identified by the pinchpoint analysis.

4.3.1 Baseline Connectivity Analysis
For the baseline demonstration, the outbreak origin was placed in a forested grid cell north of the Winterthur city centre representative of a scenario in which the disease enters through a wild boar population in that region and disperses in different directions. All five outputs were enabled, with 500 BCRW realisations and 2,000 iSSF-IBMM agents. The analysis completed in under three minutes on a standard laptop.
The LCP corridor analysis connected the outbreak origin to the nearest reachable WILMA habitat clusters via the pre-computed Dijkstra cost grid. The graduated blue styling assigned light sky blue to distant corridors serving high cummulative resistance cost, vivid blue to intermediate connectors, and deep navy to the backbone segments shared by multiple routes and smaller cummulative resistance cost. The paths concentrated in the forested ridgelines and crossed the wildlife overpasses, consistent with the visual pattern of low-resistance cells in the Zürich resistance map.
The circuit-theory pinchpoint raster, computed using Circuitscape.jl via Julia subprocess, showed concentrated current density at the defined outbreak point and at several bottlenecks. These bottlenecks included, wildlife crossings, but also narrow forest corridors that are separated from one another by roads or railway tracks between habitat patches. These pinchpoints represent the locations where a fence intervention would produce the largest reduction in connectivity at lowest material cost.
The continuous infection-risk raster produced three discrete EFSA-aligned zones around the origin. The high-risk zone (risk above 0.50) extended approximately 2.5 to 3.5 kilometres in the least-resistant directions, consistent with its calibration to the 4-kilometre mean wild boar dispersal distance. The EFSA surveillance zone boundary (risk 0.15) was reached at cost-equivalent distances of approximately 8 to 10 kilometres through continuous forest and at shorter Euclidean distances across fragmented terrain.
The BCRW density and iSSF-IBMM contamination probability layers broadly corroborated the LCP and pinchpoint structure. The BCRW density surface showed the highest visitation counts along the same corridors identified by the Circuitscape analysis, confirming their role as preferred transit routes. The iSSF-IBMM log10-transformed contamination probability surface showed the steepest probability gradients at the forest-to-infrastructure transitions where resistance increases rapidly.



Example outputs of the wildboar connectivity plugin for a simulated outbreak origin north of Winterthur. Top left: least-cost path corridors to the 100 nearest low-resistance habitat clusters, styled by cost-distance weight, with thick dark-blue segments indicating near-origin backbone corridors and thin light-blue segments indicating distant, high-cost connections. Top right: infection risk surface derived from an exponential decay function, classified into three zones following EFSA guidelines (high risk > 0.50, medium risk 0.15–0.50, low risk ≤ 0.15). Bottom left: dispersal corridor probability raster from circuit theory, where bright cells indicate pinchpoints through which movement is concentrated. Bottom right: random-walk visit density from 500 biased correlated random walks, showing the stochastic spread envelope around the outbreak origin.




4.3.2 Scenario Comparison: Virtual Fence Intervention
To demonstrate the scenario comparison functionality, a virtual fence was drawn over a wildlife overpass and a new wildlife overpass was built in the north of winterthur crossing a highway. The fence was rasterized as a two-cell-wide NaN wall in the modified resistance array and the full analysis was rerun without changing the outbreak origin or any other parameter. Both runs used identical settings so that all differences in the output layers can be attributed entirely to the fence modification.
The pinchpoint raster showed a clear rerouting of current density away from the blocked corridor segment. The cumulative flow that previously concentrated at the motorway crossing was redistributed to the new overpass, building an alternative corridor. The LCP backbone similarly shifted away from the blocked crossing to the new generated one, increasing connectivity to the south. The infection-risk zone contracted asymmetrically on the side of the fence facing away from the outbreak origin, indicating reduced modelled reachability in the fenced direction.

Left column shows the baseline scenario without interventions, right column shows the same outbreak after placement of a fence (red line) and a wildlife overpass (blue dot) on the resistance surface. The fence severs several southward corridor branches in the modified scenario, while the overpass maintains connectivity across an otherwise impassable barrier. Bottom row: circuit-theory pinchpoint rasters showing dispersal corridor probability. The fence visibly reduces current flow along the blocked routes, and the overpass creates a new high-current channel at its location, demonstrating that both barrier and crossing interventions are correctly propagated through the resistance grid before analysis.

The fence reduces the southward extent of the medium-risk zone, while the overpass opens a new low-risk finger of connectivity in that direction. Bottom row: iSSF-IBMM contamination probability surfaces (log\textsubscript{10} scale, 2000 agents). The fence visibly suppresses agent penetration into the southern urban fringe, and the overpass enables a new dispersal channel through the previously impassable barrier, reflected in the shifted spread envelope in the modified scenario.


The scenario comparison illustrates the core purpose of the plugin: rather than producing a single static map, it enables iterative exploration of management alternatives within the same GIS session. A wildlife manager can test different fence alignments, observe how each one redirects the modelled corridor network, and compare the resulting infection-risk zones, all without leaving the QGIS environment or re-running any preprocessing steps.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.1 Ecological Interpretation of the iSSF Model
This thesis set out to adapt a connectivity modeling framework for wild boar by building an empirically calibrated resistance surface, to develop an interactive QGIS plugin for testing landscape modifications, and to produce scenario-contrast visualisations for wildlife authorities in Canton Zürich. The following sections evaluate how far each objective was reached, place the findings in context, and set out the principal uncertainties.
All seven retained covariates were positive predictors of transit movement, confirming that wild boar in directed movement prefer denser forest at both scales and greater distance from every class of transport and settlement infrastructure. This matches the established ecology of the species, which depends on continuous forest cover for movement and strongly avoids traffic, light, and disturbance (Morelle et al. 2015; Guberti et al. 2019). Two features of the coefficient structure stand out. Forest density at the 50-metre scale carried by far the smallest standard error, reflecting the central role of immediate cover. Distance to railway carried a nearly identical point estimate but with a much larger standard error, most likely because railways are sparse in the Aargau training area and few transit steps were recorded near them, so the avoidance effect is real but its magnitude is less certain.
The positive coefficients at both forest scales indicate selection for cells that are locally wooded and embedded in a forested surrounding, consistent with hierarchical habitat selection (Avgar et al. 2016). The binary forest cover layer essentially acts as a coarser version of the 50-metre forest density layer and therefore adds no further information to the model. Distance to forest edge, on the other hand, does not appear to capture a pattern that is relevant to in-matrix movement. During directed transit, wild boar are not actively seeking out forest edges. Instead, they favour dense forest cover that offers continuous concealment along the route. The tendency to stay close to forest edges is more characteristic of in-patch behaviour, where animals benefit from quick access to foraging in adjacent agricultural fields while remaining within reach of cover. In addition, transit routes regularly pass through both forested and open sections, so that the distance to forest edge varies in both directions along a single path and the variable ends up carrying no consistent signal.
The non-significance of slope and terrain ruggedness can be explained by the relief of the training landscape itself rather than by a genuine lack of influence on wild boar movement. Canton Aargau and also the extrapolated canton Zurich are lowland regions with comparatively flat topography, so the variation in slope and ruggedness across the study area is small and the available GPS data may simply not contain enough contrast in these variables for the model to detect an effect. This does not mean that terrain is irrelevant to wild boar movement in general. In a landscape with hard elevation differences, steep slopes and rugged terrain, these covariantes will likely have an influence on animal movement by increasing the energetic cost of travel and by channelling routes along valleys, ridgelines or passes. A model calibrated on telemetry from such a region would likely find these covariates both significant and informative. The result obtained here should therefore be read as a property of the specific training area rather than as evidence that terrain can be safely ignored when transferring or rebuilding the model for landscapes with more substantial relief.
The weak but significant avoidance of water in the model fits well to wild boar ecology. In in-patch movement wild boar are generally drawn to water bodies for drinking, wallowing and the cover offered by riparian vegetation. However, since the model captures only the in-matrix steps, where the animals move directly between patches rather than foraging or resting, a lake or a river can represent a minor obstacle that has to be circumvented or crossed at a suitable point. This adds a small energetic and time cost to an otherwise direct path, which is enough to produce a weak preference for routes that stay slightly farther from water during fast, directional movement, even though the same animals may seek out water intensively in other behavioral states.
The consistent avoidance of railways, settlements, main roads and secondary roads during in-matrix transit shows one shared underlying behaviour rather than four independent effects. All four covariates represent sources of human presence, noise and physical disruption, and wild boar are well documented to treat such features as zones of elevated risk that they cross only when necessary. The particularly strong effect for distance to railway likely reflects both the physical hazard of crossing active tracks and the fact that rail corridors often run through open, exposed terrain that offers little cover during a crossing attempt, which is precisely the kind of situation a transiting animal would want to minimise. Distance to settlement showed a comparable pattern, consistent with the broader finding that proximity to human settlements is one of the strongest predictors of reduced wild boar occupancy and habitat use (Lee et al. 2025, DOI: 10.3390/ani15233423). Assigning dense settlements the maximum resistance in the burn-in phase rather than NoData is a deliberate compromise: wild boar do enter urban fringes nocturnally (Guberti et al. 2019; Morelle et al. 2015), so treating settlement as an absolute barrier would suppress pathways that occur in reality, and pathways routed through such cells should be read as rare but possible. The weaker but still significant avoidance of main and secondary roads fits the same logic on a smaller scale. Roads bring traffic noise, lighting and the chance of direct encounters with humans or vehicles, and although they are far easier to cross physically than a railway or a built-up area, they still represent a brief moment of high exposure for an otherwise cover-seeking species. Together, these four effects suggest that wild boar in transit actively route themselves around the infrastructure network, trading a longer or more indirect path for reduced exposure to human-associated risk, which is exactly the kind of behavioral trade-off a resistance-based connectivity model is meant to capture.
The exclusion of distance to fenced roads in the iSSF is a transferable methodological point. Including it produced an ecologically implausible apparent attraction toward motorway fencing, an artifact of animals pacing along impassable barriers and generating dense telemetry clusters. This pacing behaviour likely arises because a fenced motorway represents a hard edge in an otherwise continuous landscape. When wild boar reach such a barrier while moving along a familiar route, they do not simply turn back. Instead, they tend to follow the fence line in search of a gap, an underpass or some other point where the obstacle can be crossed, which produces repeated, movement directly alongside the infrastructure. A model that only sees the resulting concentration of GPS fixes near the fence has no way of distinguishing this search behaviour from genuine habitat preference, and ends up interpreting the barrier itself as an attractive feature. Handling such hard barriers through the deterministic burn-in rather than as a step-selection covariate is the correct response, and any iSSF study in a landscape with dense linear barriers should apply the same check before finalising variable selection.
The two movement kernel terms, log_sl and cos_ta, were both highly significant in the final model. This indicates that step length and turning angle carry genuine information about how wild boar move during in-matrix transit, beyond what is explained by the landscape covariates alone. Their significance confirms that including these terms in the iSSF was necessary. Without them, part of the habitat selection signal could have simply reflected the animal’s typical movement pattern rather than an actual preference for certain landscape features. By accounting for the intrinsic step-length distribution and the degree of directional persistence directly in the model, the remaining covariate effects can be interpreted as genuine habitat selection during transit, separated from the mechanics of the movement process itself.

title: 5  Discussion
section: 5.2 Resistance Surface Quality and Transfer Validity
text:
5.2 Resistance Surface Quality and Transfer Validity
The Aargau resistance surface reproduces the expected corridor structure, with low resistance along forested areas, intermediate resistance across the agricultural plain and high resistance in and around urban areas. The median resistance of 35.1 lies clearly above the scale midpoint of 27.8, which suggests that during transit wild boar experience most of the landscape as costly rather than neutral. This fits the broader idea of a landscape of fear, in which an animal’s route choice while moving between patches is shaped less by the search for good habitat and more by the need to minimise exposure to risk. Wild boar do not migrate by preference. Long-distance transit through open or human-influenced terrain exposes them to disturbance and potential mortality, so they undertake it only when a change of patch is necessary, and they try to keep the associated exposure as low as possible. This is also visible in the structure of the iSSF results themselves. In-patch behaviour reflects a search for the best available option within a landscape the animal already knows and uses regularly, whereas in-matrix behaviour is dominated by avoidance. Of the covariates retained in the final model, only the two forest density measures act as attractants, while distance to railway, settlement, main road, secondary road and water all represent features the animal moves away from. The asymmetry between two attracting and several avoiding covariates is consistent with a transit phase in which the priority is not to find an optimal location but to reach the next patch while passing through as little risk as possible.
Transferring the Aargau parameters to Zürich is operationally necessary because no Zürich telemetry was available, and it rests on the assumption that wild boar respond to forest and infrastructure similarly in both cantons. This is plausible given their shared Mittelland structure and the broadly consistent habitat preferences of European wild boar (Morelle et al. 2015), but the more intensively urbanised Greater Zürich landscape may host animals with modified avoidance responses that the Aargau coefficients do not capture. Reusing the Aargau scaling parameters for the z-standardisation is what keeps the beta coefficients interpretable across the transfer, since the covariates are then expressed on the same scale on which they were originally estimated. The final normalisation, however, is computed on the Zürich-specific eta range rather than the Aargau range. This choice means that the most suitable Zürich forest cells are mapped to R = 1 and the full [0, 1] suitability scale is used within the canton, which is exactly what a tool meant to identify corridors inside Zürich needs. The cost is that the resulting resistance values can no longer be compared directly to their Aargau counterparts, since a value of, 20 no longer represents the same relative habitat quality in both rasters. For a tool that is explicitly scoped to intra-cantonal spatial planning in Zürich, this loss of cross-cantonal comparability is an acceptable trade-off.
The Keeley constant of C = 4 was adopted from Fischer et al. (2024), where it was calibrated for red deer rather than wild boar. There is no published wild-boar-specific value for this exponent, and the way a species translates habitat suitability into perceived movement cost can plausibly differ between a large, wide-ranging ungulate such as red deer and a smaller, more generalist species such as wild boar. Ecologically, C controls how strongly small differences in habitat suitability are amplified into differences in movement cost. A higher value stretches the resistance scale into a steep curve, so that cells just below the suitability optimum are already treated as considerably more costly, which concentrates modelled movement into narrow corridors through the very best habitat. A lower value would flatten this relationship, letting the model treat moderately suitable areas as only slightly more costly than optimal ones and producing broader, more diffuse corridors. Because wild boar are a comparatively flexible, generalist species that is known to use a wider range of habitat types than red deer, it is conceivable that their real perception of cost rises less steeply with declining suitability, which would argue for a smaller C than the one used here. Using C = 4 is therefore a pragmatic choice rather than a species-calibrated one. It draws on a value that has already been applied successfully in a comparable connectivity modelling context and produces a resistance range that is wide enough to differentiate corridors meaningfully, but it should be read as a reasonable working assumption rather than as an empirically derived parameter for wild boar, and one that may overestimate how selective the species actually is when moving through the landscape.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.3 The Planning Tool in Context
The central advance over the static models of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023) is interactivity. Both provide rigorous maps of the current landscape but cannot answer the what-if questions that ASF management requires. The plugin closes this gap: a user can draw a fence across a pinchpoint, re-run the model, and see directly how the corridor backbone, the infection-risk zones, and the contamination surface respond. This addresses the trade-off Hess (1994) identified, where the same corridor that benefits a species can accelerate disease, by showing both sides of a specific intervention rather than a general map.
The five modules are complementary rather than redundant. Least-cost paths give the optimal routes, circuit theory reveals bottlenecks and redundancy that a single path cannot (McRae et al. 2008), the infection-risk raster expresses cost-distance as an EFSA-anchored probability that veterinary authorities can read directly, the biased correlated random walk offers an independent stochastic check that converges toward the circuit result (Saerens et al. 2009), and the individual-based model adds an epidemiological layer by simulating disease trajectories conditioned on an ASF infectious period. Using the published Circuitscape.jl solver, with settings matching Urbina et al. (2023), favours a validated implementation over a custom one, while the scipy fallback preserves the capability where Julia is unavailable.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.4 Limitations and Sources of Uncertainty
The most significant limitation is the absence of formal validation. The iSSF fit was not quantified with concordance statistics or spatial cross-validation, and predictive performance on held-out Aargau steps was not assessed, so the relationship between modeled resistance and actual movement probability remains uncertain (Avgar et al. 2016). The Zürich surface is entirely unvalidated, since no Zürich tracks were available to test the transferred corridors, which adds a layer of uncertainty to management decisions based on the Zürich map. A gap of roughly ten years separates the 2014 to 2017 telemetry from the 2026 landscape data, so infrastructure and land cover changes are not reflected in the behavioural calibration, and their net effect was not assessed. The 15-minute fix interval reliably captures directed transit (Podgórski et al. 2013; Benhamou 2014) but the conservative classifier may exclude some shorter in-matrix steps, slightly underestimating selection strength, though the large retained sample and high significance of all predictors suggest the coefficients are robust. Finally, the plugin modules carry their own assumptions: the infectious-period distribution is calibrated to Eastern European and Baltic populations (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018; Probst et al. 2017; Chenais et al. 2019) whose disease course may differ from ASF-naive Swiss wild boar, and the static movement kernel does not capture nocturnal or seasonal variation in space use.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.5 Practical Implications and Outlook
The tool is primarily a pre-outbreak planning instrument. Its main value is enabling authorities to identify high-risk corridors and prioritise fence locations before an incursion, with the pinchpoint map showing where a small barrier achieves the greatest reduction in connectivity and the infection-risk raster showing which zones would require surveillance under EFSA guidelines. The scenario comparison supports the iterative decision-making that operational management needs, letting an officer test alternative fence alignments in a single session without programming or reprocessing.
The pipeline follows the FAIR principles of the ZHAW reproducibility requirement, drawing on publicly accessible federal geodata except for the partner-provided telemetry and fence data, with the full workflow encoded in documented notebooks and the plugin distributed as an installable QGIS package reusable in other cantons. Three extensions would add the most value. The highest priority is obtaining GPS telemetry from Zürich wild boar to validate the transferred surface against independent movement data. A seasonal decomposition of the iSSF would reflect the substantial behavioural shifts between winter mast foraging and the active season (Morelle et al. 2015). Finally, weighting the outputs by estimated wild boar density would add the host-abundance dimension that, together with connectivity, drives epidemic spread (Guberti et al. 2019).

section: A.2 Telemetry Data Quality and Exclusions
text:
A.2 Telemetry Data Quality and Exclusions
The raw telemetry comprised 36 GSM-GPS deployments recorded at a nominal 15-minute fix interval. The following cleaning and exclusion steps were applied before any movement statistics were computed. The first five days of each deployment were removed as a capture-shock buffer. Deployments with fewer than 100 fixes or spanning less than 30 days after cleaning were excluded. One deployment, 027_Agat_13970, was removed because it was a short re-collaring of an animal already represented by a longer deployment (027_Agat_13969) and retained only 50.6 percent of its scheduled fixes. After duplicate collapse, the remaining deployments retained at least 90 percent of unique scheduled fixes, yielding 132,388 classified steps of which 7,810 were in-matrix transit steps.

title: Appendix A — Data Sources and Input Datasets
text:
A.3 Detailed Layer Processing
This section records the dataset-specific processing decisions that were condensed in the methods chapter, so that the pipeline remains fully reproducible.
swissBOUNDARIES3D (version 1.5, swisstopo). Administrative geometries were extracted from the TLM_KANTONSGEBIET polygon feature class. The dataset has a stated geometric accuracy of about ±0.5 metres in position and elevation. Extracted cantonal geometries were buffered by 2,000 metres and converted to a rectangular processing extent, passed as a Well-Known Text filter to the vector reading functions to load only intersecting geometries.
swissTLM3D (2026 edition, swisstopo). Forest was taken from the tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung layer, retaining closed forest (“Wald”), open forest (“Wald offen”), scrub (“Gebueschwald”), and woody areas (“Gehoelzflaeche”), and excluding unstocked forest, mining areas, orchards, cemeteries, vineyards, and water-body areas. Roads from tlm_strassen_strasse were classified into fenced high-performance roads (“Autobahn”, “Autostrasse”, “Ausfahrt”, “Einfahrt”, “Zufahrt”, “Autozug”), main roads (“10m/8m/6m Strasse”), and secondary roads (“4m/3m Strasse”, “2m Weg”, “Verbindung”, “Dienstzufahrt”, “Platz”). Settlements used the tlm_namen_siedlungsname polygon classes “Ort”, “Ortsteil”, “Quartier”, and “Quartierteil”, preferred over building footprints because wild boar respond to the contiguous built-up matrix. All linear features were reduced to two dimensions on import. A prep_above_ground() function removed subsurface segments using the STUFE vertical-position attribute (retaining values of zero or greater) and the KUNSTBAUTE attribute (removing “Tunnel”, “Unterfuehrung”, “Unterführung”, “in Gebaeude”, “in Gebäude”, in both ASCII and Unicode spellings). A clean_railways() function removed out-of-service lines and funiculars, rack railways, and heritage lines. Binary presence rasters used all-touched rasterisation, and Euclidean distance rasters were computed for each class.
Forest structure. A binary forest mask, a 50-metre and a 1000-metre circular focal-density layer, and an unsigned distance-to-forest-edge layer were derived from the forest mask. The two density layers represent the immediate (micro-canopy) and macro-scale orders of habitat selection.
Water. Standing water from tlm_gewaesser_stehendes_gewaesser was reconstructed from three-dimensional shoreline multi-line strings into polygons (Z dropped, grouped by gwl_nr, unioned, line-merged, cast to polygons), with island polygons subtracted. Lakes above one square kilometre were held as absolute barriers. Flowing water from tlm_gewaesser_fliessgewaesser retained only surface-level features (verlauf of “Oberirdisch”, “Bruecke”, or “Wasserfall”), excluding piped and subterranean streams. A combined distance-to-water layer was computed as the cell-wise minimum of the two components.
DHM25 (swisstopo). Slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index were derived at the native 25-metre resolution. The DHM25 is referenced to LV03 (EPSG:21781), assigned manually before processing, and was reprojected to LV95 by bilinear interpolation. Its vertical accuracy is about ±1.5 metres on the Swiss Plateau and ±3 to ±8 metres in Alpine terrain, and its altitude data were surveyed between 1952 and 1979 with final updates in 1999, so recent terrain alterations are not represented.
Wildlife passages (FOEN, N2023). The N2023_Version_Wildtierpassagen polygons were reprojected to LV95, buffered by 30 metres, and rasterised so that verified crossings override the barrier effect of fenced motorways.
Permanent ASP fences (Cantonal Veterinary Office Zürich). The Dauerzaeune.shp woven-wire fences were rasterised and burned in as absolute barriers in the Zürich surface only.
WILMA core habitats (December 2024). The Potenzial_Wildschwein_Kerneinstaende_ZH_2024_WILMA.shp layer delineates predictive potential resting habitats and was used as a spatial validation anchor and as least-cost-path targets, not as confirmed animal presence.

B.1 Final iSSF Coefficients
This appendix collects the full statistical output of the integrated step-selection function and the parameter settings of the five plugin analysis modules, so that the results in the main text can be reproduced and audited.
The final conditional logistic regression was fitted on 7,810 in-matrix transit steps from 36 GPS-collared individuals in Canton Aargau, each compared against ten random control steps. All covariates are z-standardised with the Aargau training mean and standard deviation. The seven retained coefficients, ordered by magnitude, are reproduced in ?tbl-issf-coefficients in the results chapter and summarised here for reference: forest density at the 50-metre scale (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.513\)), distance to railway (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.513\)), forest density gradient at the 1000-metre scale (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.245\)), distance to settlement (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.224\)), distance to main road (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.218\)), distance to secondary road (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.149\)), and distance to water (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.051\)). All coefficients were positive and significant at the 0.05 level, and all variance inflation factors for the retained set were below 1.4.
