title: Appendix B — Statistical Outputs and Model Parameters
text:
B.3 Plugin Analysis Parameters
The five analytical modules of the Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin use the following fixed parameters. The analysis window extends 11,500 metres in each direction from the outbreak origin (a 10,000-metre buffer plus a 1,500-metre edge buffer). The infection-risk kernel uses the published mean natal dispersal distance of European wild boar of 4 kilometres, with the EFSA protection zone (3 km) and surveillance zone (10 km) mapped to risk thresholds of 0.50 and 0.15. The biased correlated random walk uses a von Mises concentration of \(\kappa = 2.0\), a 2,000-step limit, and 500 realisations by default. The iSSF-based individual movement model runs 2,000 agents by default, draws the infectious period from a \(\text{Gamma}(\alpha = 3, \beta = 3.5\,\text{days})\) distribution (mean 10.5 days), and generates 25 candidate steps per move using a gamma step-length kernel (shape 2.653, scale 160 m) and a von Mises turning kernel (\(\kappa = 1.064\)).

B.5 Excluded Covariate Layers

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.3 The Planning Tool
The central advance over the static models of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023) is interactivity. Both provide rigorous maps of the current landscape but cannot answer the what-if questions that ASF management requires. The plugin closes this gap: a user can draw a fence across a pinchpoint, re-run the model, and see directly how the corridor backbone, the infection-risk zones, and the contamination surface respond. This addresses the trade-off Hess (1994) identified, where the same corridor that benefits a species can accelerate disease, by showing both sides of a specific intervention rather than a general map.
The five modules are complementary rather than redundant, and the baseline run shown in @fig-plugin-comparison illustrates both their value and their respective caveats side by side. The least-cost path panel traces a clear backbone radiating from the outbreak origin toward the surrounding habitat destinations, giving an immediate overview of where the landscape is currently most permeable. As an overview tool it works well, but the single traced route should not be mistaken for a realistic depiction of how an actual animal moves, since no wild boar has complete knowledge of the cost surface across an entire canton and travels the literal cheapest line from origin to destination. Circuit theory contributes exactly the perspective a single path cannot, revealing bottlenecks and redundancy in the corridor network [@mcrae2008], and the pinchpoint panel concentrates current density into a small number of bright branches that mark the structurally most important crossings. At the same time, the brightest of these branches in this run follows the valley floor where the basemap shows the corridor passing close to settled ground rather than staying within forest cover, a direct illustration of how the method’s sensitivity to the way resistance values combine across parallel and series paths in the underlying resistor network can make a route through the edge of a built-up area register as the dominant pinchpoint, even though it is not a route a wild boar would ever take. This means the pinchpoint layer has to be read alongside the land cover rather than taken at face value. The infection-risk raster expresses cost-distance as an EFSA-anchored probability that veterinary authorities can read directly, but this strength comes with a limit of its own: insofar as the EFSA zone radii are fixed regulatory distances rather than empirically derived thresholds, a continuous surface calibrated to reproduce those same radii mainly shows how the irregular landscape reshapes an idealised circular buffer rather than supplying a genuinely new estimate of risk, and the panel makes this point visually, since the three zone boundaries closely follow the terrain instead of forming the regular rings a fixed-radius rule would draw. The biased correlated random walk offers an independent stochastic check that converges toward the circuit result at the theoretical limit [@saerens2009], and the corresponding panel shows a dense, well-defined core directly around the origin. It also shows a faint halo of thin trailing paths extending well beyond the forested ridge into the more open and settled terrain to the south and east, which is exactly the kind of drift away from the expected forest corridor that suggests the cost and persistence weights alone do not always keep the walk on ecologically plausible paths, with the stochastic component occasionally overriding the pull of the landscape. The individual-based model adds an epidemiological layer by simulating disease trajectories conditioned on an ASF infectious period, and its panel is the most telling of the six in one particular respect: alongside the contiguous high-probability zone immediately around the origin, a second, clearly separated cluster of low-probability cells appears further to the southeast with no continuous path of finite resistance connecting it to the main mass. Because the agents in this model select their next step purely by endpoint suitability without checking whether the straight line to that endpoint crosses an impassable cell, an infected agent can occasionally appear to step across a barrier such as a motorway or a large lake that should be entirely impermeable, and this detached cluster is best read as a visible instance of that artifact rather than as a real, independently reached focus of contamination. Using the published Circuitscape.jl solver, with settings matching Urbina et al. (2023), favours a validated implementation over a custom one, while the scipy fallback preserves the capability where Julia is unavailable.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.5 Practical Implications
The tool is primarily a pre-outbreak planning instrument. Its main value is enabling authorities to identify high-risk corridors and prioritise fence locations before an incursion, with the pinchpoint map showing where a small barrier achieves the greatest reduction in connectivity and the infection-risk raster showing which zones would require surveillance under EFSA guidelines. The scenario comparison supports the iterative decision-making that operational management needs, letting an officer test alternative fence alignments in a single session without programming or reprocessing.
The pipeline follows the FAIR principles of the ZHAW reproducibility requirement, drawing on publicly accessible federal geodata except for the partner-provided telemetry and fence data, with the full workflow encoded in documented notebooks and the plugin distributed as an installable QGIS package reusable in other cantons.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.6 Outlook
Several extensions would add further value to the pipeline.
On the methodological side, the step classification could be revisited using Hidden Markov Models. This approach was explored during the project and then set aside, both because of its added complexity and because the rule-based classifier already produced convincing, interpretable results at much lower implementation cost. An HMM-based classification could still serve as an independent validation of the current rules or as a refinement in a future iteration of the pipeline.
The covariate set itself also leaves room for improvement. A true forest density layer derived directly from canopy data would likely outperform the proxy used here, and several infrastructure-related variables could be made more realistic, including the width and passability of rivers, traffic volume on roads as a proxy for disturbance intensity, and a distinction between small settlements that wild boar can and do cross and larger urban areas that act as effective barriers.
Because the cantonal boundary is an artificial cut in an otherwise continuous landscape, incorporating spatial data from the adjacent German border region would help reduce the edge effects that currently limit the validity of the resistance surface near the northern cantonal edge.
The model would also benefit from a stronger temporal dimension. A seasonal decomposition of the iSSF would reflect the substantial behavioural shifts between winter mast foraging and the active season (Morelle et al. 2015), and a day and night distinction could capture the marked differences in wild boar activity and risk perception between these periods, both of which are likely to shape transit routes in ways the current single, season-pooled model cannot represent. Agricultural and crop-related factors were deliberately left out of these considerations, since they primarily influence in-patch behaviour rather than the directed transit movement this model focuses on.
Finally, two extensions remain particularly important for moving from a methodologically sound prototype to an operationally validated tool. The highest priority is obtaining GPS telemetry from Zürich wild boar to validate the transferred surface against independent movement data. Beyond that, weighting the outputs by estimated wild boar density would add the host-abundance dimension that, together with connectivity, drives epidemic spread (Guberti et al. 2019).

title: 2  Theoretical Background
text:
2.3 Wild Boar Ecology
The wild boar (Sus scrofa) is a native Eurasian ungulate whose European populations have expanded strongly in recent decades, driven by milder winters, the spread of maize and other high-energy crops, reduced hunting pressure, and supplementary winter feeding (Guberti et al. 2019). Wild boar are habitat generalists that use woodland, especially deciduous and mixed forest, as daytime resting cover and forage at night in agricultural fields, showing marked behavioural flexibility in fragmented and peri-urban landscapes (Morelle et al. 2015). This forest dependence for cover and avoidance of human infrastructure is what a resistance surface must capture. Home ranges are usually well below 50 square kilometres and movement contracts where food is stable and abundant (Guberti et al. 2019; Morelle et al. 2015). The epidemiologically important exception is natal dispersal by young males, which can cover much greater distances and, rarely, exceed 100 kilometres (Guberti et al. 2019), because a dispersing animal in the incubation phase can carry infection into previously unaffected areas.
Movement ecology commonly separates an animal’s trajectory into two distinct behavioural states that alternate as it moves through a heterogeneous landscape: localized, resource-oriented behaviour within a habitat patch, and directed, fast transit between patches across the surrounding matrix. In-patch movement is characterised by short steps, frequent changes in direction and extended residence time, reflecting activities such as foraging, resting or social interaction within an area the animal already knows and uses regularly (Podgórski et al. 2013). In-matrix movement, by contrast, consists of comparatively long, directionally persistent steps that connect separate patches and minimise the time spent in less suitable surrounding terrain (Clontz et al. 2021). The distinction matters for resistance-based connectivity modelling because such models are meant to represent the cost of moving between habitats, so they should be calibrated on the transit portions of the telemetry record rather than on the localized behaviour that otherwise dominates it. Identifying these transit segments from raw GPS data by combining step length and turning angle thresholds, and requiring several consecutive steps to meet these criteria before classifying a sequence as directed transit, is an established way of separating genuine in-matrix movement from isolated long steps that can arise from GPS measurement noise (Benhamou 2014).
